articles.title: Two New Games Coming to Apple Arcade's Growing Puzzle Catalog
articles.subtitle: Apple today announced that "Block Blast!+" and "Art of Fauna: Cozy Puzzles+" are coming to Apple Arcade on September 3, adding two more puzzle games to the service's catalog.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
Apple today announced that "Block Blast!+" and "Art of Fauna: Cozy Puzzles+" are coming to Apple Arcade on September 3, adding two more puzzle games to the service's catalog.

Block Blast!+ is the Arcade edition of " Block Blast," a chart topping block clearing puzzle game. Players fill a grid with block shapes to clear full rows and columns, chasing bigger combos as they go, and the Arcade version drops the ads found in the free to play original.

Art of Fauna: Cozy Puzzles+ is based on " Art of Fauna: Cozy Puzzles," winner of the 2025 App Store Award for Cultural Impact. Players reconstruct vintage style nature illustrations piece by piece while learning facts about the animals depicted, and the game offers a text based alternative to the visual puzzles for players with visual or cognitive impairments.

The two new titles join an existing roster of Arcade puzzlers, including the dungeon crawling combat puzzler " Grindstone," the pipe connecting puzzle game " Flow Free+," and the word search title " Crossword Jam+." " Everyday Puzzles: Mini Games+ " and "Water Sort Puzzle: Get Color+" are more recent additions to that same catalog.

A handful of existing Arcade games are also gaining new content this month. On August 12, " puffies. " adds 28 new packs, including two collections themed around Oden Tomodachi and The Knights. Starting August 20, " Simon's Cat - Blast Time " is rolling out 200 new levels, with 50 arriving each week over the course of a month. And on August 26, " stitch. " hits a milestone of 800 unique hoops, marked with a commemorative hoop and a new achievement.

September 3 brings a wider wave of additions to Arcade beyond the two new puzzlers. " NFL Retro Bowl '27 " also gains its new Gauntlet Mode that day, tasking players with stringing together as many consecutive wins as possible using limited starting resources, with real NFL players and more perks the further they progress.

"Coloring Games for Families+" launches with more than 3,000 activities aimed at players of all ages, while " Let's Play! Oink Games+ " brings nine of the developer's board games to Arcade, supporting solo play, offline multiplayer, and online matches.

‌Apple Arcade‌ is a subscription service that provides access to hundreds of games across the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple TV, and Apple Vision Pro. All of the games are free of ads and in-app purchases. In the U.S., ‌Apple Arcade‌ costs $6.99 per month, and it is also bundled with other Apple services in all Apple One plans. ‌Apple Arcade‌ can be accessed through the ‌App Store‌ and the Apple Games app.

articles.title: Apple releases rare ‘point’ betas for iOS 26.6 and macOS 26.6
articles.subtitle: Macworld Typically, Apple issues operating system updates to beta testers only for major point releases, such as iOS 26.5 or macOS 26.6.
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Typically, Apple issues operating system updates to beta testers only for major point releases, such as iOS 26.5 or macOS 26.6. The minor-level point releases with two decimal points (e.g., macOS 26.6.1) generally bring little more than bug fixes and security updates that are pushed to users without any beta testing from developers or the public.

It’s unusual, then, that Apple just pushed out iOS and iPadOS 26.6.1 along with macOS 26.6.2 to beta testers. The number discrepancy is because macOS just got a 26.6.1 release to fix a security vulnerability that only affects macOS. The release notes state these new 26.6.1/26.6.2 betas only include security fixes, but they don’t say what they are. Apple does not update its Security Release page for beta releases.

It’s unclear whether these were published to the beta site by mistake or if Apple has some reason to test this small update in the wild. At any rate, it should release to the public within a week or two. Without knowing the content of the release, we can’t say how important it is yet.

If you’re in the beta test group, you can update to this latest version by opening Settings > General > Software Update.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

articles.title: Claude chats exposed in Google searches – another endorsement of Apple’s privacy approach
articles.subtitle: We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
We’ve long cautioned against disclosing sensitive personal data in AI chatbot sessions, given that most companies use these as training data, but there’s now an even bigger reason.

Things got way worse over the weekend when Redditors discovered that you could access some Claude AI chats through a simple Google search …

Claude chats exposed

Claude has a share option that allows you to share a chat session with a colleague, friend or family member. The chatbot generates a link you can send to one or more individuals, and Claude implictly assures you that nobody can see the chat knowing the URL.

To share a chat: Click the “Share” button in the upper right corner of your chat. Once a chat has been shared, anyone with the link can view the chat snapshot.

The problem is that Redditors discovered you don’t in fact need the link to be able to view the chat. You can simply Google for it, either using specific search terms or just asking Google to show you all of the chats that have been shared in this way. BBC News reports:

Hundreds of user conversations with Anthropic’s popular artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot Claude were found to have been available to essentially anyone online […] Users on Reddit initially discovered, external the publicly available chats, which covered more than 200 conversations with Claude across at least 25 pages of search results – some taking place just weeks ago.

Literally all you had to do was tell google to search the directory used for shared Claude chats (site:claude.ai/share).

As you might expect, some of the chat sessions were completely unhinged, like asking why the record industry was hiding the fact that birds co-wrote most of Jay-Z’s albums. But others contained extremely sensitive information, such as transcripts of private conversations; a lawyer asking if they needed to self-report a breach of conduct; and a user asking for help creating a crypto wallet, and exposing their keys in the process.

Anthropic has so far attempted to claim that this is not a problem.

When someone shares a conversation, they are making that content publicly accessible, and like other public web content, it may be archived by third-party services.

The reality, of course, is that it is very much a problem, since this is not at all what users would expect. Worse, a Wired reports suggests that the underlying cause appears to be gross incompetence.

WIRED reviewed a sample of the exposed Claude chat pages and found that they did not include the “noindex” tag that both Bing and Google say they take into consideration when deciding whether or not to index a page […] Anthropic didn’t respond to questions about why it didn’t include the “noindex” tag on the shared chat pages.

It follows yesterday’s news about Claude Cowork being able to escape its sandbox on Mac and gain full access to all files.

How to protect yourself

The problem appears to have been at least partially addressed for now, with previously available search results now failing, but I would advise against using the share feature given that it relies on security by obscurity.

I’d also advise removing any past shared chats. You can do this in Settings > Privacy > Shared chats > Manage.

Another endorsement of Apple’s approach

articles.title: GTA 6’s $100 Ultimade Edition Has More Pre-Orders Than the Standard Game
articles.subtitle: Fans are willing to pay a premium for Rockstar's anticipated game Related When it was announced that Grand Theft Auto 6 's standard edition would cost $80, some felt that was too high a price even for the most anticipated video game of all time.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Fans are willing to pay a premium for Rockstar's anticipated game

Related

When it was announced that Grand Theft Auto 6 's standard edition would cost $80, some felt that was too high a price even for the most anticipated video game of all time. However, it now seems that plenty of people are willing to spend even more than that on Rockstar's open-world adventure as we get closer to release.

In an interview with CNBC, Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick revealed that GTA 6 's standard edition is not selling equally to the $100 Ultimate Edition. "Actually," Zelnick said, "it is skewing more to the premium edition." While that sounds like great news for Rockstar and Take-Two, Zelnick is more realistic about what that statistic could reveal about pre-release hype for the game. "That might be a reflection of the fact that the most avid consumers are the ones who are pre-ordering," the executive explained.

Earlier in the interview, Zelnick admitted that while Take-Two had "a great deal of pricing power" with GTA 6, the company wanted the cost to be a relative value. "We understand that a consumer experience is the intersection of the thing itself and what you pay for it," Zelnick said, continuing that "We would never want people to feel like this is out of my range.

" This echoes comments from Zelnick during a Take-Two earnings call earlier this week, in which he called GTA 6 an "incredible bargain" at its standard $80 price point.

When asked what players get in the $100 edition of the game, Zelnick simply stated, "Additional content. " The official pre-order page for the game details this further. Pre-ordering the Ultimate Edition unlocks a slew of exclusive cosmetics and a free month of GTA+, the subscription service that grants players perks in GTA Online.

Throughout the interview, Zelnick reiterated that Take-Two expects GTA 6 to do incredibly well but doesn't want to set expectations too high. In discussing how the game might sell over time, Zelnick referenced the company's track record with GTA 5 's historic sales of over 200 million copies since the game's release in 2013. In the context of GTA 6, Zelnick said he'd "never project that to occur again. "

GTA 6 will be released Nov. 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X.

articles.title: Recovery Key storage transition highlights Apple’s privacy and obscurity
articles.subtitle: We trust Apple with a lot of our data. In general, that hasn’t seemed like a bad idea; in particular, compared to its competitors, Apple seems to ensure that it can inspect or interact with very little of our data.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
We trust Apple with a lot of our data. In general, that hasn’t seemed like a bad idea; in particular, compared to its competitors, Apple seems to ensure that it can inspect or interact with very little of our data. The company has built its platform and its reputation on being an elegant, frictionless, hands-off conduit.

While we can make many complaints about Liquid Glass, its increased focus on invasive (and poor) advertising, its software quality, and much else, Apple has kept its corporate nose cleaner than anybody else. Its transparency and documentation are, oddly, worse than its actions and clear intent.

I was thinking about this when I received an email from an anonymized iCloud Hide My Email account, asking for more detail about how Apple managed the transition from the old method of presenting or escrowing (in iCloud) your macOS FileVault Recovery Key to the new method, in which the key is stored in Passwords. This transition, which I’ve documented in a few places, was a step forward in privacy and security.

But not transparency! I’ll explain, but you can’t find an explanation on Apple’s site about the transition. The support documentation remains out of sync with Tahoe. That leaves it to yours truly to explicate.

Don’t trust and verify

The Electronic Frontier Foundation recently published a newsletter with a round-up of how fitness wearables, like rings, watches, and bands, preserve your privacy from government intrusion, as well as whether they protect you from unwanted security invasions by using end-to-end encryption (E2EE). (The former often requires the latter: governments typically can’t break through E2EE.)

I want to quote two full paragraphs to make this point:

In the end, we found that only four of these companies (Apple, Google, Whoop, and Oura) promise to notify users of law enforcement requests in publicly available documentation. And just two of those companies, Apple and Google (which also owns Fitbit), currently publish transparency reports on how often they hand users’ data to the government.

Support for end-to-end encryption—a method that ensures your personal data is only accessible by you, and not the company who makes the device and manages the cloud storage—is more rare than transparency reports among wearable device makers. The Apple Watch is the only popular fitness wearable that supports end-to-end encryption. 1

And just two of those companies, Apple and Google (which also owns Fitbit), currently publish transparency reports on how often they hand users’ data to the government.

Support for end-to-end encryption—a method that ensures your personal data is only accessible by you, and not the company who makes the device and manages the cloud storage—is more rare than transparency reports among wearable device makers. The Apple Watch is the only popular fitness wearable that supports end-to-end encryption. 1

Apple wasn’t an early player with E2EE. Really, it was seen as the kind of thing only true security geeks cared about, even while people like EFF and other digital privacy advocacy groups and individuals warned us that our data was only lightly protected. Over time, as the criminal, exploitative, and political monitoring and extraction of our secrets became clear, Apple kept stepping up.

The Secure Enclave is a keystone of those moves, as the tamper-resistant silicon subsystem allows devices to keep locally generated security keys entirely private. Most of these keys never leave the Secure Enclave! Rather, it’s the encryption hub. 2

iCloud initially had a fairly cursory level of protection, with the then-Apple ID account password serving as the only real bar. Two-step verification in March 2013 provided better account protection, but didn’t cover iCloud backups, which could be retrieved without that second step. A rash of celebrity account leaks in late summer 2014 led Apple to extend two-step to iCloud data within a couple of weeks.

The next year, it upgraded security to the more rigorous two-factor authentication, which later became mandatory.

As part of its response to the iCloud data hijacks, Apple began to beef up iCloud. It began rolling out E2EE for all the device-based services it could, leaving synced data still relatively lightly protected. (iCloud data is always encrypted with Apple’s at-rest keys, which only it ostensibly has access to, and in transit with HTTPS. However, a security breach at Apple or someone able to hijack one end of an in-progress HTTPS sync allows access to that unencrypted data.)

Then, suddenly, months after shipping major updates to its operating systems, Apple announced Advanced Data Protection in December 2022. Enabling this feature put the E2EE aegis over nearly all synced or stored data at iCloud; mail, contacts, and calendar entries remain an exception because of their interoperability with third-party apps and services. You can view Apple’s document that explains what level of protection applies to data, with and without ADP enabled.

With that in mind, let’s talk about the Recovery Key transition.

articles.title: MacPaw is building an on-device AI layer that will work across your Mac apps
articles.subtitle: MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac. The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac.

The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.

MacPaw is teaming up with Liquid AI to bring more on-device AI to the Mac

Liquid AI’s Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) will be adapted for Mac-based assistance and combined with MacPaw’s own on-device technologies: Mnemos for memory and Elix for inference.

Eney already shifted to a local model last year, keeping reasoning, contextual search, skill execution, and conversation history on the device whenever possible.

The new partnership is intended to push that approach further. The two companies are jointly developing the underlying stack rather than MacPaw simply adding another third-party model.

Once the technology has been tested and implemented in Eney, MacPaw says it plans to bring it to more of its products. It also wants to make the shared AI stack available to Mac developers through Setapp.

That could let participating apps expose more of their capabilities and context to Eney. This would allow the assistant to understand what is inside an app. It could also provide more useful answers or take relevant actions.

articles.title: AAPL stock rallies 15% as investors favor AI caution and welcome price increases
articles.subtitle: Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Apple stock slid significantly downwards in the wake of the WWDC keynote, with some attributing that to disappointment in the company’s AI announcements.

While we disagreed with that analysis, investors do now seem to be welcoming the company’s caution when it comes to AI spending, with the stock rallying 15% since that June low …

The company’s shares slid 4% the day after the keynote, but there were a number of macroeconomic factors affecting a wide range of stocks at the same time, including US strikes against Iran after the downing of an American helicopter.

The stock has rallied even more substantially since then, pushing it back into record territory. Bloomberg believes that AI is a factor in this, albeit somewhat indirectly. It suggests that investors are growing increasingly skeptical about AI spending by other companies and says that Apple’s more cautious approach is now seen as a positive.

The stock’s reversal reflects rising unease about the prospects for heavy spending on AI paying off, with Apple’s decision not to participate in the data center arms race increasingly being viewed as an asset, rather than a liability, even though its AI offerings have repeatedly frustrated investors.

“There’s a battle in the market, and right now Apple is benefiting because it isn’t in the storm that the rest of the AI trade is in,” said Mark Bronzo, chief investment strategist at Rye Strategic Partners. “People are concerned about what kind of return hyperscalers could get from their AI spending [and] as a result, investors have gravitated back to Apple as a steady-eddy name without those risks. ”

Asus Armoury Crate is not my favourite bit of software. It looks all high-tech on the surface, but any time I use it for more than five minutes, I'm reminded of the fact it's rather messy. It's also hit the headlines previously for patched security vulnerability issues—and good news, folks, here we go again.

Per the Asus security advisory board, Armoury Crate, Asus GPU Tweak III, and GPU Tweak II should all be updated to ensure "optimal protection," after the discovery of a new security vulnerability.

Listed as CVE-2026-8917, the issue has been given a score of 8.4 out of 10, with a "high" severity rating. Which is, funnily enough, the exact same rating as the previous issue we wrote about last year. "An IOCTLY vulnerability allows a local attacker to write a specific value to an arbitrary memory address, potentially leading to privilege escalation," says the posting.

Well, that sounds like something that should be patched up at the earliest possible moment. The CVE listing doesn't mention Armoury Crate specifically, but the Asus page mentions that "a component used" by the software is part of the update, so time to get installing.

GPU Tweak III, II, and AI Suite 3 will need the latest versions installing from their respective support pages, whereas Armoury Crate can be updated from within the app itself.

As an aside, Asus isn't the only company that patches out security vulnerabilities for its software on a regular basis, so if you've got something hanging around in your system tray from another hardware provider (particularly system/mobo software that came with your machine), it's a good idea to check for updates on a regular basis.

It's a dangerous world out there, and new security holes are patched all the time. Get thee to the update menu, and keep your ear to the ground.

Apple’s future OLED iMac could use a new five-layer display panel that LG Display is developing to improve brightness, extend panel life, and reduce the risk of burn-in during long periods of use.

The Elec reports that LG Display is working on a five-stack OLED structure with blue, green, blue, red, and blue emitting layers. Its current high-resolution monitor panels use four layers, so the extra blue layer would help spread the electrical load across the display.

That matters because high-resolution OLED panels use very small pixels, and manufacturers need to push more current through those pixels to maintain brightness. Higher electrical load can shorten panel life and increase the chance of image retention, especially on desktop displays that often show static menus and app interfaces for hours.

Apple is targeting a brighter OLED iMac

Apple reportedly asked LG Display and Samsung Display for information about OLED panels for a future 24-inch iMac last year. The company discussed a panel with 600 nits of brightness and a pixel density of 218 PPI, while the current 24-inch iMac uses an LCD panel rated at 500 nits.

LG Display has also developed a 27-inch 5K OLED panel with a 220 PPI RGB stripe layout, although that panel appears to serve mainly as a test for high-density OLED production rather than a direct iMac component.

The five-layer design adds manufacturing cost because it requires more organic material and a more complex deposition process, so LG still needs to meet Apple’s brightness and lifespan targets while keeping yields under control.

articles.content:
Wispr Flow users on Mac can now access Notetaker, an AI-powered meeting assistant that uses calendars, connected apps, and personal dictionaries to provide additional context for transcripts, summaries, and notes. Here are the details.

Wispr Notetaker now available for Mac

If you’re unfamiliar with Wispr Flow, it is one of the leading voice-to-text AI tools for a growing number of users who feel comfortable using voice to compose messages, emails, documents, and other text instead of typing.

Granted, voice-based interactions are not practical in every environment. Still, Wispr Flow ’s rapidly growing user base (which the company said in March was expanding by 40% month over month) suggests that AI-powered dictation tools may become mainstream faster than many expected, or give them credit for.

Until now, Wispr has offered a single product, which polishes up messy speech and turns it into “clear, polished writing in every app.”

Today, the company is expanding its lineup with Notetaker, a smart, AI-powered meeting assistant, transcriber, and summarizer. The new tool is built directly into Wispr Flow and appears as a new item in the app’s left-hand sidebar.

As Wispr CEO and co-founder Tanay Kothari notes (no pun intended):

“Nobody reads meeting transcripts. But everyone acts on them. The transcript feeds the summary, the summary feeds the follow-up email, the recap goes to whoever missed the call. You’ve learned to give the notes a quick once-over before trusting them, because sometimes a name is wrong or an action item is assigned to the wrong person.”

In other words, while the transcript itself may have limited value to some, accurately extracting the key details, decisions, and action items from it can be more useful to a broader set of users.

Notetaker also briefs users before meetings by gathering relevant information from their notes and the web, with each line linked to its source. More broadly, it draws context from calendars and connected apps such as Slack.

During meetings, Notetaker provides a live transcript so the user can quickly check back on what was said. Once the meeting ends, it processes the full recording again with additional context, which Wispr says improves the final transcript and the summaries, decisions, key dates, and action items generated from it.

Afterward, users can ask questions about their full meeting history, with answers linked to the moment when the relevant information was discussed. Notetaker can also catch users up on portions of a meeting they missed or were not paying attention to.

In addition to sharing Wispr Flow ’s custom dictionary, which helps with accuracy for acronyms, names, product names, and beyond, Wispr Notetaker “draws on the apps you connect, like Slack, and your calendar, to understand what this particular conversation is about,” says Kothari.

This also helps with automatic speaker attribution, which is particularly useful for meetings with several participants.

Wispr Notetaker transcribes meetings based on on-device audio capture, rather than joining calls as a separate participant.

It works across multiple meeting platforms, including Zoom, Google Meet, Teams, and Slack huddles, and has MCP support, allowing users to pull transcripts, summaries, and notes into Claude, ChatGPT, and custom agents or workflows.

Wispr Notetaker is available beginning today on Mac, with a Windows version in development.

articles.title: 7 Of Deadpool’s Best Fighting Game References In Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls
articles.subtitle: Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls Before Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls was even out, fans spotted dozens of fighting game references in Deadpool’s character guide.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls

Before Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls was even out, fans spotted dozens of fighting game references in Deadpool’s character guide. Wade Wilson is known as a fourth-wall-breaking gremlin, so you would naturally expect him to have a few nods to pop culture in his dialogue, but Tōkon ’s stuffed the guy’s red suit full of references to not only Marvel and fighting games writ large, but also the history of the fighting game community.

YouTuber Dan Allen Gaming has put together two videos showcasing all the references fans have found thus far, and Deadpool’s kit is really just an amalgamation of so many different fighting game characters.

Some elements come from series like classic Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, and Tekken, but there’s also a swath of homages to various games in developer Arc System Works’ catalog like Guilty Gear and Dragon Ball FighterZ. If you want to see them all, you can check out both of Dan Allen Gaming’s videos, but here are a few favorites we wanted to highlight.

Dropping an arcade cabinet on fools like Liu Kang / Woshige’s infamous EVO blunder

One of Liu Kang’s fatalities in the Mortal Kombat series has the fighter dropping a whole Mortal Kombat arcade cabinet on his enemies. In those games, the cabinet smashed Liu Kang’s foes to a bloody pulp, and perhaps if Tōkon was just a Deadpool game instead of a broader, T-rated Marvel one, it might have done so here, too. But alas, the Deadpool cabinet that falls from the sky just knocks downed foes to the side a little bit.

Also found in this sequence is a reference to the 2015 EVO moment where Guilty Gear Xrd Sign player Woshige preemptively celebrated winning a match before realizing there was still another round. Deadpool imitates Woshige’s pop-off before scrambling to get to the arcade cabinet that falls on his enemy, just as Woshige did at EVO.

The dramatic fall of Fatal Fury ’s Geese Howard

If Deadpool is defeated while in the air, he will dramatically fall in a way that’s different from how most characters are knocked out in Tōkon. That’s because it’s a reference to an iconic win scene from Fatal Fury, in which antagonist Geese Howard falls from a tower into a chasm below. This moment would be recreated in several games that followed, and now Deadpool is throwing his mask into the ring of “people falling dramatically in fighting games.

Cell’s intro recreated with practical effects

Deadpool’s intro when he’s leading a fight is a callback to Cell’s intro in Dragon Ball FighterZ. While the Dragon Ball villain begins battles by charging himself up with a powerful aura that surrounds him, Deadpool merely imitates the visual of this by setting off a firework behind himself and striking the pose.

A long-lost PlayStation icon

One of the more bizarre references Deadpool has is to Polygon Man, an old PlayStation mascot that Sony quickly shelved in the ‘90s in favor of more marketable faces like Crash and Spyro. articles.title: Is Apple’s affordability balancing act about to come crashing down?
articles.subtitle: Macworld Apple, despite its reputation, has never been a luxury company. Macs and iPhones may cost more on average than their competitor’s counterparts, but when you compare apples to Apple’s, a MacBook Pro or iPhone 17 Pro is worth spending a few dollars...
articles.author: Macworld Reviews
articles.content:
Apple, despite its reputation, has never been a luxury company. Macs and iPhones may cost more on average than their competitor’s counterparts, but when you compare apples to Apple’s, a MacBook Pro or iPhone 17 Pro is worth spending a few dollars more for than a comparable model from HP or Samsung.

Since its very first computer, Apple’s mission has been clear: build the best computer it can at a reasonable price. That’s not necessarily the cheapest product (and quite honestly, often isn’t), but the one with the best mix of features, performance, and build quality for the price.

Buying a new iPhone or MacBook shouldn’t be a difficult decision—if you’re willing to pay Apple’s prices, you’re getting a device that looks nicer, performs great, works with all your other Apple devices, and lasts longer. It’s a balancing act that relies on all aspects of Apple’s development process to be in sync.

But over the past couple of months, that has begun to shift. In late June, the company was forced to raise prices on all Macs and iPads due to the worsening RAM crisis, including the MacBook Neo, a laptop that epitomized Apple’s pursuit of value so perfectly, it even exceeded Apple’s own lofty expectations. What was seen as the sign of a new era for Apple’s affordability now costs 20 percent more than it did when it launched in March and suddenly isn’t an impulse buy.

Now it looks like that balancing act will get a little more precarious when Apple launches its new iPhones next month. Not only is Apple expected to raise prices on iPhones, but the highly anticipated folding iPhone Ultra will likely start at $2,000 or more. And suddenly, Apple’s carefully crafted balancing act could come crashing down.

Tipping the scales

In a way, this all started with the iPod. When it launched in 2001, it cost $399 for 5GB of storage, the same price industry-leading Creative charged for its Nomad Jukebox that had four times the storage. Naturally, the iPod was seen as overpriced, outmatched, and downright laughable–until people got to use one and discovered that Apple got everything right.

The form factor, transfer speeds, sound quality, and navigation were all superior to the Nomad Jukebox, and it didn’t take long for the iPod to become the most popular mp3 player.

And then Apple did something somewhat uncharacteristic–it expanded the line with cheaper models. Within four years, there was the $249 mini, $149 nano, and $99 Shuffle, basically an iPod for every budget. It was a strategy that paid off, turning the iPod into a cultural sensation with some 500 million sold.

When Apple followed up the iPod with the iPhone in 2007, there was a similar sticker shock. It started at $499 with 4GB of storage or $599 for 8GB of storage with a 2-year Cingular contract (rebranded AT&T Mobility just before the iPhone went on sale), about double what other so-called smartphones cost.

But the iPhone was a repeat of the iPod: It quickly proved its worth, cheaper models followed, and the industry shifted. Apple repeated the formula with the iPhone X, pushing the starting price to $999 for the first time, then keeping the price steady and offering cheaper options alongside it.

But nine years later, Apple is at a crossroads. While the RAM crisis has spared the iPhone thus far, there are numerous signs that Apple is set to launch its most expensive iPhone Pro line ever, with prices set to rise $100-$200 across the board, and even more for higher-end storage options. To make matters worse, Apple is reportedly delaying the base iPhone 18 until the spring.

That means there won’t be a new iPhone this holiday season that costs less than $1,200–and we don’t know yet if Apple will increase prices for the 17 and 17e.

It could be all too much for Apple’s balancing act. The iPhone 18 Pro is essentially an S-year model with a higher price tag, while the iPhone Ultra will be a first-gen product that merely looks like an overpriced Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 clone.

Even with higher trade-in values, the Apple Upgrade program, and whatever exclusive Siri AI features are tied to the new phones, Apple is in real danger of selling fewer new iPhones than ever before. Apple fans have grown accustomed to a certain level of stability with iPhone prices, and after Apple already raised prices on the MacBook Neo, nothing is off the table.

Just a couple of months ago, 2026 was shaping up to be the year when Apple’s slow march up the mountain of affordability finally reached its zenith. Now it looks like it all might come crashing down.

It’s the end of a very short road for ChatGPT Atlas, OpenAI’s dedicated web browser for Mac. OpenAI has shared details about what happens when ChatGPT Atlas shuts down this weekend.

ChatGPT is the new ChatGPT Atlas

As we reported in July, OpenAI is discontinuing its standalone Atlas browser in favor of browser tools built into the new ChatGPT desktop app. Atlas is scheduled to stop working on August 9 following a brief wind-down period.

OpenAI warns that Atlas may no longer open, browse, or support agentic workflows after that date. Because the discontinued browser will not continue receiving security updates, users will want to move to a supported alternative.

The transition may require some manual housekeeping for some. Atlas bookmarks will not transfer automatically. OpenAI recommends exporting bookmarks as an HTML file and saving important pages before Sunday’s deadline.

Cookies may have export options where available. ChatGPT conversation history is stored separately and will remain available.

AI browser alternatives

OpenAI is directing users toward the new ChatGPT desktop app. Its built-in browser supports multiple tabs, downloads, website logins, autofill, password management, extensions, and persistent browser state. However, it’s not exactly a browser-first experience.

The company recommends its Chrome extension when a task requires an existing Chrome profile, signed-in session, open tabs, or other extensions. ChatGPT’s desktop app also includes a “computer use” functionality that can optionally let it control Safari when granted permission.

There are plenty of other AI browser options on the Mac, including Comet, Dia, Opera Neon, and Aside. Anthropic is taking a similar two-track approach: Claude Code offers a sandboxed in-app browser, while its Chrome extension can work with existing logged-in sessions.

articles.title: Siri will sometimes summarize webpages and videos from within Safari and YouTube apps
articles.subtitle: Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari. Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex … The Siri...
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Although the Siri app refuses to summarize webpages, the intelligent assistant can do so from within Safari.

Similarly, it can summarise the content of YouTube videos from within the app – though the exact situation with both appears complex …

The Siri app refuses to summarize URLs

In the first developer beta, the Siri app would not summarise the content of a URL pasted into it. However, it would not explicitly refuse. This behavior changed in beta 2, with an explicit refusal.

A new section in Siri AI’s system prompt now says: “You cannot access content behind a URL. When a user provides a URL and asks you to summarize, read, or extract information from it, inform them that you cannot access web pages. Do not offer follow-up suggestions or workarounds.”

We speculated that this may be a deliberate decision on the company’s part in order to avoid robbing websites of visitors, which would make the web increasingly unsustainable over time.

Siri in Safari and YouTube will sometimes summarize

However, if you are inside the Safari app and ask Siri to “summarize this,” then it will do so at least some of the time. Other times, it will say it’s unable to do so.

It’s the same story inside the YouTube app, where Siri will sometimes summarise a video and other times say it is unable to do so.

9to5Mac’s Take

Given these differing behaviors, it’s not entirely clear what Apple intends the assistant to do in response to these requests. The fact that it’s a developer beta makes it harder still to differentiate intended behaviors from unexpected results, and we can expect further changes in future betas.

When we use the thumbs down feedback response, we can see a report which includes most of the sources used to answer the question. In the case of our own YouTube video, Siri has the 9to5Mac video channel as part of its world knowledge index, so it’s likely to be gathering the information from that. However, there are other occasions when it is very definitely examining the live webpage content – for example, reading a comment that has only just been posted.

We’ve reached out to Apple and will update with any response.

Get ready for 2026's most anticipated FPS

If you play first-person shooters but you haven't heard about Wardogs yet, now's the time to get clued up because it finally has a release date: developer Bulkhead's new game will be coming to Steam Early Access on Thursday, Sept. 10, and it will cost $39.99.

This news follows the recent closed alpha which took place from Aug. 7-9, and had outstanding player feedback online, much like the previous playtest. FPS content creator TheTacticalBrit thinks it could be "incredibly successful," noting that it has "wow moments" in a "pick-up-and-play" format, unlike other shooters geared towards realism.

Meanwhile, another creator, GhostGamingGG, claims that flying helicopters in Wardogs "absolutely destroys Battlefield 6 's air mechanics." A third, Melandryu, considered the weekend to be "one of the best experiences" they've had with a beta in "many, many years" (it was technically an alpha, but the message is the same).

If you pre-order Wardogs, you'll also be able to partake in an upcoming closed beta weekend, taking place from 21-23 Aug. According to a press release, "the beta will give players the opportunity to experience the game ahead of its early access launch and put its large-scale warfare, servers and core systems through their paces."

Wardogs is aiming to fill the niche between FPS games that are considered to be more casual, such as Call of Duty and Battlefield, and more realistic, hardcore games, such as Squad and Escape From Tarkov. In development by Bulkhead, previously of Battalion 1944 fame, it's aiming to do things a little differently.

For example, you can become an arms dealer by selling weapons to your teammates. In-game cash is a major part of Wardogs, and this mechanic allows you to essentially run a business. When I spoke with the Wardogs' CEO, Joe Brammer, he explained that this is an FPS for " dad gamers," because everything you do in-game, whether you're actually killing enemies or not, still contributes to the team effort. It also has permanent progression, where XP is earned by your actions, like in RuneScape.

articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Pastebot’s Quick Menu.

Tapbots has released Pastebot 3, a ground-up rewrite of the Mac clipboard manager that includes several powerful automation and customization options, along with two new pricing models.

Pastebot was already one of the Mac’s best clipboard utilities, capable of managing an extensive collection of copied text and images in multiple formats, PDFs, URLs, files, and HTML, along with metadata. The app can handle up to 1,500 clippings and features fast search, extensive customizable keyboard shortcuts, list and detail views of clipboard items, and iCloud sync between multiple Macs.

Pastebot 3’s main menu.

What sets Pastebot 3 apart is its addition of deep automation tools. Not only does the update add MCP support, making it an excellent tool to use with Claude or ChatGPT/Codex, but it includes a brand new CLI that you or an agent can use from Terminal or incorporate into scripts you build. Commands include:

List available Pastebins

Browse and search clipboard history

Filter results by Pastebin or date

Retrieve the full text of a clipping

Retrieve images from clippings

List available Pastebot filters

Apply filters to clippings or supplied text

Place an existing clipping on the clipboard

Create new text or image clippings

Paste clipboard contents into the frontmost app

Delete individual clippings

Clear the main clipboard history

Filters.

articles.subtitle: Apple today shared a 90-minute WWDC26 presentation recorded live at a packed Steve Jobs Theater, featuring impressive demos of its latest AI tools for developers and an entire app built from just a few prompts.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence

Apple today shared a 90-minute WWDC26 presentation recorded live at a packed Steve Jobs Theater, featuring impressive demos of its latest AI tools for developers and an entire app built from just a few prompts. Watch it below

Live session held at the Steve Jobs Theater during WWDC26 now available

The Apple Developer YouTube channel shared an interesting 90-minute WWDC26 session today called “ Inside Apple Intelligence and Xcode: Special Presentation. ”

While parts of the presentation can get technical, after all, this is a WWDC session, the video offers very interesting insight into what developers will be able to build using the new technologies, frameworks, and APIs it announced during the event.

Perhaps one of the more interesting parts of the video is a 20-minute segment in which an entire app is built from a single prompt and then further tweaked with follow-up commands.

The result is a WWDC badge tracker app featuring 3D animations, holographic effects, and even Visual Intelligence capabilities—all created from just a few prompts.

Along the way, the demo highlights new Xcode 27 features that come into play before coding begins, including asking clarifying and follow-up questions and mapping out the project in advance.

The session continues with demos and valuable information on how apps can integrate with the new Siri AI, how developers can leverage the new Apple Foundation Models framework, and, in turn, how the framework integrates with the new Core AI framework and the upgraded MLX framework, even when using third-party models.

The special presentation ends with an impressive demo of the 1-trillion-parameter Kimi 2.6 model running locally in LM Studio across four Mac Studios, using the low-latency RDMA-over-Thunderbolt technology Apple introduced with macOS Tahoe 26.2.

articles.title: Supermassive Games are the latest studio to announce layoff plans, with 75 jobs at risk just three months after Directive 8020 launch
articles.subtitle: The Dark Pictures Anthology: Directive 8020 It’s the developers' third round of redundancies in two years Until Dawn and The Dark Pictures Anthology devs Supermassive Games have announced the beginning of redundancy consultations for up to 75 of its staff,...
articles.author: Rock Paper Shotgun
articles.content:
The Dark Pictures Anthology: Directive 8020

It’s the developers' third round of redundancies in two years

Until Dawn and The Dark Pictures Anthology devs Supermassive Games have announced the beginning of redundancy consultations for up to 75 of its staff, a process that will almost certainly add to the thousands of layoffs endured by the games industry over the past few years.

Posted on Not Twitter earlier today, the announcement of these imminient cuts comes just three months after Supermassive’s most recent horror adventure, Directive 8020, and contains wording that’s uncomfortably reminiscent of the studio’s last round of mass redundancies in July last year. That, too, followed a previous round in early 2024, in which an estimated 90 workers at the UK-based studio lost their jobs.

"This is a necessary step to help ensure the sustainability of the company," the most recent livelihood-axing JPG argues, while assuring that it was a "difficult decision" to begin the consultations. Last year’s announcement called it a " very difficult decision," mind, so I guess it must have been slightly easier this time around.

A statement from Supermassive Games. pic.twitter.com/Vom1CSGYGs — Supermassive Games (@SuperMGames) July 22, 2025

A statement from Supermassive Games. pic.twitter.com/Vom1CSGYGs

"We know this will be an incredibly difficult time for everyone, and our priority throughout the process will be to provide support to all those impacted."

In fairness to the difficult decision makers at Supermassive – so, so difficult, which is why they’ve made it thrice – they’re far from alone in maintaining that staunch executive-class belief that surely, more can be made with less.

Other recent mass cuttings range from ZA/UM laying off 30 developers just after the launch of their Disco Elysium successor Zero Parades, all the way up to Microsoft slashing thousands of roles as part of their great studio sell-off.

In the past week alone, Crossfire studio That’s No Moon dropped 14 members of staff, Quantic Dream faced calls for strike action over the negotiation process for its planned 115 job cuts, and Halo: Campaign Evolved devs Halo Studios celebrated the FPS remake’s launch by ending the employment of a 6-year senior contractor.

See how difficult it is?

articles.title: Apple’s new Foundation Models explained: on-device AI, cloud AI, and everything in between
articles.subtitle: During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
During the WWDC26 keynote, Apple announced its third generation of Apple Foundation Models (AFM), comprising five models, some of which are local, some of which are cloud-based, and one of which lives in Google’s servers running on Nvidia chips. Here’s a breakdown of how that will work.

A bit of background

When Apple first announced its foundation models in 2024, the lineup included an on-device language model with roughly 3 billion parameters, and “a larger server-based language model available with Private Cloud Compute and running on Apple silicon servers,” as the company put it at the time.

Private Cloud Compute was an ambitious undertaking, as it aimed to deliver cloud-based AI capabilities while preserving the same privacy guarantees users expect from on-device processing.

For this reason, keeping everything in-house was essential. Private Cloud Compute ran in Apple data centers, on servers powered by Apple silicon. Even so, its privacy guarantees could be independently verified by third-party security researchers.

However, as Apple struggled to get its AI aspirations off the ground, the company partnered with Google to use Gemini as the backbone of its new AI efforts, the results of which it announced earlier this week during the WWDC26 keynote.

Apple’s new foundation models

The third generation of AFMs includes five models: AFM 3 Core and AFM 3 Code Advanced, which are on-device models, and AFM Cloud, ADM 3 Cloud (Image), and AFM 3 Cloud Pro, which are server-based. The D in ADM 3 Cloud (Image) stands for diffusion, a technology we’ve covered in the past here.

Except for AFM 3 Cloud Pro, all other models were built to run on Apple silicon devices. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, meanwhile, runs on NVIDIA GPUs hosted in Google Cloud.

This was made possible afer Apple extended its Private Cloud Compute architecture to third-party infrastructure for the first time, “while maintaining Apple’s powerful security and privacy protections,” according to the company.

As for the models themselves, here’s a breakdown of each one, as explained by Apple:

AFM 3 Core, the next generation of our 3-billion-parameter dense model that delivers a step up in quality. AFM 3 Core Advanced, our most powerful on-device model. It’s natively multimodal, enabling helpful features like expressive voices and higher-accuracy dictation.

Built on cutting-edge Apple research, this 20-billion-parameter model uses a sparse architecture, activating just 1 to 4 billion parameters at a time depending on the request. AFM 3 Core Advanced is unlocked by and optimized for our most capable Apple silicon systems. AFM 3 Cloud, our server-side workhorse, optimized for speed, efficiency, and performance.

ADM 3 Cloud (Image), for image generation and editing, which unlocks advanced photo-editing tools, the all-new Image Playground, and more. AFM 3 Cloud Pro, our most capable server-based model, which powers our most demanding use cases, like agentic tool use and complex reasoning.

articles.title: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls Commits a Cardinal Video Game Sin
articles.subtitle: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls commits a fighting game cardinal sin Related There’s a lot to love about Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls — at least now that its PC performance issues are resolved.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls commits a fighting game cardinal sin

Related

There’s a lot to love about Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls — at least now that its PC performance issues are resolved. It makes great use of heroes like Spider-Man and Blade to create fighters with diverse movesets. It sports stylish art that captures the essence of both comics and anime. And its matches are full of dramatic reversals, making for a great spectator sport. There’s just one problem: I’m still struggling to remember what the heck every button combination does.

Yes, Marvel Tokon carries on a time-honored fighting game tradition, in that it contains a lackluster tutorial that throws a lot at you at once. It’s fine for genre veterans who know the dance by now, but it puts a barrier on a game with more mainstream appeal than your typical fighter. I’m not asking for much; I’m just begging for one good onboarding experience in my life.

Marvel Tokon teaches you the ropes in a long-winded tutorial that walks you through every single thing you can do in the game. Blocking, Link Attacks, Assemble Assists — you’ll execute every move at least once in your first half-hour. How well will you retain any of it? Well, that’s a different story.

While I hit all the right marks in the tutorial, a lot of moves quickly faded from my brain by the time I started playing through Tokon ’s single-player story. I could remember the basic combos and I knew how to attack with my heroes in reserve, but I couldn’t keep the finer details straight. What did pressing these two buttons at the same time do again? How do I counter an attack?

Wasn’t there a second counter, too? It’s like being told a 12-digit number sequence and having to hold it in your memory for hours before you can punch it into a computer. (Maybe I’m just revealing something about my short-term memory here, but surely someone reading can relate! )

This is a recurring issue for me as someone who casually enjoys fighting games. I similarly struggled to find my sea legs in Invincible Vs, which has a similarly bare-bones tutorial. Simply telling me what a button does and then having me press it three times against a stationary enemy isn’t a great way to learn.

It rarely gives me a sense of the actual context I’d use that move in, and context is everything in a fighting game. I either find myself constantly referring back to the tutorial or a menu when trying to learn a fighting game, or just remember what I can and make the most of those moves until I naturally learn to use something I’d forgotten about.

I’m sympathetic to fighting game tutorial designers, of course. They have the unenviable task of trying to explain dozens of complicated systems in a quick manner that lets players get to the fun so they can start experimenting. No one wants to be stuck in a long tutorial! But after struggling to get started in another great fighting game that otherwise feels built for me, I’m once again hungry for creative solutions.

I can’t pretend to know the solution, but for my money, Street Fighter 6 is still my north star. Say what you will about its Yakuza-like World Tour mode as a single-player offering, but it's an incredibly effective teaching tool. The mode gradually introduces new techniques in side-missions as the story progresses, giving you time to learn a move and then put it into practice before being taught something new.

That gave me time to commit each new move to memory, and I could hold my own in online matches as a result… Well, I could at least get a few punches in before getting air juggled, at least.

Even if its tutorial is insufficient, I’m planning to push on with Marvel Tokon anyway. It’s the rare competitive fighting game where you can button mash your way into cool combos, and that motivates me to learn how to play more deliberately. Once I actually figure out how to pull off an Assemble Counter on purpose, it’s over for y’all.

articles.title: How can you run code that hasn’t been notarised?
articles.subtitle: How can you run apps and executable code that hasn't been notarised? Can you also run those with broken signatures, or none at all? And do the controls actually disable Gatekeeper or XProtect?
articles.author: The Eclectic Light Company
articles.content:
Since Apple made notarisation a requirement for those developing for macOS, it has made it progressively harder to run code that hasn’t been notarised. Prior to macOS Sequoia, one method used by those who often ran code that hadn’t been notarised was to disable Gatekeeper checks including on-demand checks made by XProtect for evidence of malware.

That was performed using the command spctl --master-disable to modify the global state of the assessment system. However, according to man spctl that is no longer supported. This article looks at what you can do now, following up from my previous testing.

There are currently three controls available:

Enter sudo spctl --master-disable, then enable the Anywhere option added to the Allow applications from menu in Privacy & Security settings.

Install a profile setting EnableAssessment to false.

Add the app(s) to the Developer Tools list in Privacy & Security settings, which allows apps to run software locally that doesn’t meet system security policy.

As the first two appear to behave identically, only the first and last are discussed here.

To ensure assessments were independent and not influenced by previous exposure to the test apps, an otherwise identical and fresh Tahoe 26.6.1 virtual machine was used for each of three sets of tests, the first without any change made to Gatekeeper or XProtect, the second after setting permitted apps to Anywhere, and the third after adding each app to the Developer Tools list.

To evaluate their effects I doctored three different apps of mine so that

one had a changed Info.plist breaking its signature,

another had its signature completely stripped using codesign, leaving it unsigned,

the third had its original signature stripped, and it was then resigned using an ad hoc signature.

None of the three apps had previously been run in that VM in any form, so were completely novel to its security and protection systems. Each app was first tested when in quarantine, then without any quarantine xattr attached.

This app was blocked from being run in every condition. When launch was attempted with the app in quarantine, the user was invited to have the app moved to the Trash, otherwise macOS simply reported that the app couldn’t be opened.

As completely unsigned code has never been allowed in Apple silicon Macs, the unsigned app behaved the same as that with a broken signature, except in one condition. When it was in quarantine and Anywhere had been allowed in Privacy & Security, an incorrect dialog was shown asking the user whether they were sure they wanted to open the app. However, that still blocked the app and reported that it couldn’t be opened after all.

As expected, without making any changes to controls, this was directed to the Trash when I tried to launch it from quarantine. When not quarantined, it launched normally, without any warning dialog.

With Anywhere allowed and in quarantine, a warning dialog was shown asking the user whether they were sure they wanted to open it. Confirming that resumed a normal launch. When not quarantined, it opened without any warning being shown.

Adding the app as a Developer Tool had a different result: when in quarantine the dialog proposed moving the app to the Trash, and offered no option to run it. However, without a quarantine xattr it opened without any warning being shown.

articles.title: Running Simulators Inside Claude Code for Mac
articles.subtitle: Claude Code has a new simulator button. Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
Claude Code has a new simulator button.

Claude Code’s Mac desktop app has added Apple simulator support, and although it’s billed as “iOS Simulator Support,” it actually works with any iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, or watchOS simulator you have installed.

The process of setting up a simulator is simple. A new button with an iPhone icon appears when you open an existing project. Click it and a new iPhone simulator pane opens to the right by default. However, clicking on the name of the simulator reveals a list of every available simulator. You can also run multiple simulators at once, but that immediately made my aging M1 Max Mac Studio start to chug a little.

With access to your running app, Claude Code is more effective at debugging UI bugs.

Once you have the simulators that you want open, simply ask Claude Code to run and test your app, and it gets to work, building the app, installing it in the simulator, opening it, and poking around. I loaded up a simple word game I’ve been playing with, and after a few minutes, Claude Code found a UI bug while controlling the simulator. I asked it to fix the issue, which it did, then tested and committed. My testing has been limited, but so far it looks like a simple, effective loop.

It’s also worth noting that Claude Code is running the simulator directly inside the Claude app. This is not computer use, meaning windows aren’t going to be opening and getting in your way as you work on something else. All in all, the addition of the simulator, like the inclusion of an in-app sandboxed browser a couple of weeks ago, is a great update to Claude Code.

On the heels of Apple’s WWDC keynote this week, Greg Joswiak and Craig Federighi sat down with Laurie Segall on the Mostly Human podcast. That's no lie. The videogame industry is in upheaval, and thousands of developers are being let go every year, seemingly irrespective of the success of their work; veteran Brenda Romero said earlier this year that "we were there in the '80s for the crash, and this is definitely crashier."

articles.title: App report: Listen, read… checkmate
articles.subtitle: Your voice may be your passport, as a certain Robert Redford picture once asserted, but two macOS apps in our spotlight this week view your voice as a way to get more things done on your Mac.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
Your voice may be your passport, as a certain Robert Redford picture once asserted, but two macOS apps in our spotlight this week view your voice as a way to get more things done on your Mac. We’re talking transcription apps with two apps that take very different approaches to what you can do with vocal recognition and AI.

But that’s not all for this week. We also look at a tool to help you better enjoy email newsletters, an iPhone app for making your photos sound as good as ever and a multiplatform game that helps you fine-tune your puzzle-solving skills.

Got an app of your own that you’d like to see highlighted? Let us know at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of what it does, and we’ll take it from there.

Vox Dictum

I record a lot of interviews, which means I need to transcribe a lot of interviews, and so far, I’ve found the Apple Intelligence tools built into Apple’s various software platforms to be fairly wanting in this area. So when an app like Vox Dictum promises a better transcription experience, I’m all ears.

Vox Dictum is a macOS app that makes privacy its calling card — all the transcription happens directly on your Mac, as do the AI-powered summary features that you can access with the cost of a subscription. A Pro subscription costs $7.99/month and gets you features like large AI models to download to your Mac plus AI summaries while the $12.99/month Pro+ package adds a speaker recognition feature.

I do think it’s easier to label speakers in VoxDictum than with any of Apple’s built-in features, though transcripts — while fairly accurate — feature line breaks that aren’t necessarily suited to my purposes.

As for the summary feature, I found it to be hit-and-miss: Vox Dictum did a great job highlighting the main points of an interview I conducted for a freelance article, making the summary a good reference tool, but a recorded discussion between me and my wife produced a summary with conflicting dates on some action items. That said, I do like that Vox Dictum’s summary feature lets you designate if the recording is an interview, a meeting, a news bulletin or a podcast, which seems to help focus the summary.

Processing time can take a bit, but if you find yourself needing to transcribe a lot of interviews, Vox Dictum is definitely worth a download so you can see if its base features improve on your current approach.

Bonfiyah

Like Vox Dictum, Bonfiyah promises to turn recordings into transcripts, while also recognizing who’s saying what. But transcription is really just a sideshow in this case — the app’s real strength lies in its ability to track your conversations.

Available for the iPhone, iPad and Mac — I tried out the macOS version — Bonfiyah records conversations, meetings and brainstorming sessions. (You can also import audio files into the app. ) Besides transcription and speaker identification features, the app also taps into AI to summarize action items that come up in your conversation and who’s responsible for taking care of them.

A feature I particularly like is an analysis tool that analyzes how to communicate more effectively with the people you talk to on a regular basis.

Transcription does take place off-device via AssemblyAI, though Bonfiyah deletes that info from its servers after seven days. The app includes privacy features such as marking conversations as privileged.

Bonfiyah comes across as a pretty sophisticated tool that might be overkill for anyone who needs transcripts with more basic summary features. But you can try out all the features to start with for 14 days before you need to commit to either a $24.99/month Pro or $34.99/month Pro AI account for more advanced features.

Letterboxx

Letterboxx exists under the premise that an email inbox is no place to enjoy a newsletter and a traditional mail client is not a reader app. Inboxes are places for taking action like responding to timely messages, but newsletters are something that you want to spend time diving into — hence the Letterboxx interface, which is designed to use the ample space provided on your Mac.

With Letterboxx, you can redirect newsletters sent to supported email accounts to a dedicated reading space, complete with folders for organizing incoming missives by type. You also get ad-filtering tools, ways to highlight relevant text and even shortcuts for managing your many subscriptions.

articles.title: macOS 27 Golden Gate: The MacStories Public Beta Preview
articles.subtitle: The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The public beta of macOS 27 Golden Gate is out today, and I’m sure many of you are wondering whether to take the plunge and give it a try in advance of its official fall release. That’s the question this preview is here to help answer.

It’s not my final take on Golden Gate by any means; after all, I’ve only been using it for about a month, and there will be several more turns in the beta cycle between now and the public release. However, I’ve used Golden Gate long enough to help you make an informed decision about whether or not to install the public beta now.

Of course, it’s impossible for me to account for everyone’s unique Mac setups when considering Golden Gate’s stability, but it’s worth reiterating what I’ve said in past previews: modern Apple betas have been consistently stable. That’s to say, the risks of using the public beta are modest. It’s been years since I’ve had a critical app fail or lost data.

I never go into beta season without a backup plan, though. If something goes terribly wrong, I have backups, backups of those backups, and alternate Macs I can switch to in the event of a disaster. I don’t expect to have to go to Plan B, but if you’re going to jump on the Beta Bus, you should have a Plan B, too.

Okay, you’ve been warned. Let’s get to the fun part.

Supported By

Inoreader

Every year’s macOS update is a little different, but Golden Gate is more different than most. Instead of focusing on tentpole features and apps (with the exception of a new Siri app), macOS 27’s updates fall into three broad categories:

refinements to Apple’s Liquid Glass design language,

hundreds of system-level changes intended to improve your Mac’s performance, and

Apple Intelligence, which includes the new Siri app as well as many other AI additions to existing system apps.

It’s been a while since the “Snow Leopard Moment.”

With so many past macOS updates focusing on system apps, it’s refreshing to see Apple take a more holistic system-level approach, which harkens back to how most people remember OS X Snow Leopard. In fact, during WWDC briefings, Apple representatives likened the Golden Gate update to Snow Leopard before anyone in the room even asked about it.

Snow Leopard is remembered as a release that focused on performance over features. The reality is that the update also introduced its fair share of new features, but many were less splashy from a user-facing standpoint. They were under-the-hood updates that made the Mac work better without users having to think about it much. In that sense, Golden Gate has a lot in common with Snow Leopard.

Other than the brand new Siri app, you probably won’t notice that much is different when you first launch the new version. But over time, the changes will reveal themselves, adding up to a whole that – with few exceptions – is greater than the parts.

So let’s take a closer look at how Liquid Glass has evolved, the most significant system changes, and what it’s like to use Siri and other Apple Intelligence updates in Golden Gate’s public beta.

Design

Windows stand out from each other more, and the sidebar runs edge to edge in Golden Gate.

A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Review: “Ted Lasso” returns, refreshed, to the pitch
articles.subtitle: Tanya Reynolds and Jason Sudeikis in “Ted Lasso.” “Ted Lasso” is back on Apple TV, which was no sure thing after the series more or less wrapped up in May of 2023.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
“Ted Lasso” is back on Apple TV, which was no sure thing after the series more or less wrapped up in May of 2023. But it’s back for a fourth season, in which—after an episode-long visit to Ted’s home of Kansas City—the football-turned-soccer coach returns to Richmond, where—as teased at the end of season 3—a new women’s team is launching and just might need a coach.

I’ve seen the first half of the season, and I’m happy to report that though the teams have changed, this is still “Ted Lasso” through and through. Thematically the first three seasons were about Ted’s journey in running away from a dissolving marriage. With season four, a whole new set of themes begin to emerge.

Yes, love ’em or hate ’em Ted’s homespun aphorisms still abound. The relationship between owner Rebecca and marketing genius Keely continues to be as strong as ever. Higgins is still doing his Higgins stuff. Mae is still tending bar. Those three fans in the pub are as random as ever.

But in coaching a barely-formed women’s team that is in desperate need of players and fans, “Ted Lasso” returns to its roots as an underdog story, which helps make the whole thing feel more like the show’s first season. (There’s even a press conference scene that is disastrous for entirely different reasons from the original. )

It’s great to have series co-creator Brendan Hunt back as Coach Beard, but the addition of Tanya Reynolds (“Sex Education”) as Alice Chilton introduces a new dynamic. Chilton is the only coach who can go into the locker room without permission, she thinks she deserves the managerial job, and she’s got some serious anger control problems. Reynolds adds a lot of grit to the proceedings, preventing it from becoming too much of a sickeningly sweet reunion love-fest.

The character least served from the season, at least so far as I’ve seen, is breakout character Roy Kent (Brett Goldstein). He’s there and has some moments, but since he’s the manager of the men’s team, he’s often relegated being a gruff, bearded question mark attached to questions about his relationship status with Keeley.

I appreciate the ironic turnabout of the men’s manager being an afterthought who’s only relevant in terms of his romantic storylines, but I do wonder if Roy is too strong of a character to be served in such limited doses.

Anyway, the best review I can give to season four of “Ted Lasso” is that each episode made me laugh out loud, a lot. Not only was it nice to see these familiar characters again, but the show did the most important job any comedy has—it’s funny. Welcome back, coach.
