articles.title: Soulver 4 casts a wider calculating net
articles.subtitle: The almost-natural-language notepad calculator Soulver’s latest release adds better tools for calculating durations or intervals between dates and times, planning travel itineraries, tracking inflation, finding distances, performing bandwidth math, and...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
The almost-natural-language notepad calculator Soulver’s latest release adds better tools for calculating durations or intervals between dates and times, planning travel itineraries, tracking inflation, finding distances, performing bandwidth math, and splitting restaurant bills or other expenses. That’s not all, but a good starting list. Should it do all these things? A point we could argue about!

But many of the features it offered in the past, and several of the new ones it provides, previously required one or more web searches to find a tool or to pull together disparate information. That’s welcome.

Soulver 4’s release comes at an interesting time, when many people have turned to chatbots and Google’s search dialog—and soon will turn to Siri AI—to answer questions that are better written out or spoken than described as just numbers or operators.

This significant update succeeds in bringing a sort of authoritative basis to stuff you need to calculate or convert. Behind the scenes, there’s no inference or autocompletion—it’s numbers, baby, all the way down. However, the developers aren’t unaware of the AI glow-up. They’ve addressed it in an interesting way, making it easy for agents to ask questions of Soulver!

How many bushels in a peck as I travel a furlong faster than a parsec?

Soulver has filled a gap for me in my calculating needs since I dug into the subject in 2015. While I love PCalc and use it for regular and advanced calculator needs, Soulver is where I go when I need to mix things up. 1

PCalc and Soulver offer overlapping Venn diagrams of what’s possible in number space, but they are distinctly different beasts at heart. Where PCalc mostly calculates within a calculator-style interface, Soulver mostly offers a way to make sense of numbers, units, percentages, time, intervals, and much more. I think of it as a “take stuff in various units or other formulations and then produce an output in a way I want” tool.

I sometimes go days without using Soulver, and then find myself typing in an array of calculations. For instance, as a tiny print book publisher (it’s just me), I am often dealing with the weight of paper, the weight of books, the cost of shipping, and other variables.

The number of sheets I have in some of my Numbers documents is alarming, but I often need conversion that sounds like a story problem: “The printer in Canada is giving me paper weight in gsm (grams per square meter). I know the book’s area per page (typically in inches). I need to calculate the weight of 1,000 copies in pounds. ” I can type the query faster than I describe it.

For instance, I need to estimate the weight of a new book based on the weight and page count of one I am holding:

(6 inches x 9 inches) / (5.875 inches × 8.25 inches) × (352 / 204) × 302g in lbs

Version 4 continues to offer all of what I consider its basics. You type out numbers and units with operators between them. You can set variables, add comments, and drag results into subsequent lines as part of further calculations. You can force-convert units, as above, telling it to use a metric unit instead of imperial, or to use a different unit scale. Say you want inches instead of feet, or kilograms instead of pounds.

Because it’s a notepad, your work is persistent. You can use Soulver to create the equivalent of tabs within sheets, collected into a “sheetbook.” This is somewhat like the Notes app, and it lets you organize calculations into projects and sub-projects. I have a monolithic sheet I use for essentially everything. Soulver can store files locally or sync via iCloud.

Where version 4 starts to diverge from previous releases is in what feels like a baroque set of options that aren’t stapled on, but most require a bit more effort to get the nuance and make them work for you.

How much did Minions & Monsters make in 1940 dollars?

It took me a few weeks to write this review, quite honestly, because every time I looked at the upgrade page, my eyes glazed over as I thought about how to best present this. I mean, the release notes page is broken into ten sections. The answer—which didn’t require Soulver 4—is that I need to cherry-pick more than usual for an app to give you the flavor.

Here are a few new elements that will keep me away from search engines and other resources more than any other:

Inflation calculation. As a historian, and as somebody who just wants to use his numeracy to interpret the world, I find myself jumping for an inflation calculator all the time. 2 You need an online source, as it has to have a table of the historical values to provide the correct cumulative percentage between two years or dates.

articles.title: Apple’s AI announcements: One big question, and 11 key features
articles.subtitle: Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form. The company had a lot of ground to make up.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apple Intelligence
articles.content:
Almost two years after Apple first showed off a video promoting the new Siri and lots of exciting new Apple Intelligence features, that future has finally arrived – at least in first beta form.

The company had a lot of ground to make up. Obviously, the test will be how well the new features work in real life usage, but let’s start with what seemed to me to be the most important things the company announced …

The big iPhone support question

For me, one of the biggest questions to arise from the keynote was exactly what features will require the iPhone 17 Pro and up?

Apple had three things to say about iPhone support. The first says that any phone capable of running iOS 26 can be upgraded to iOS 27. That means all the way back to the iPhone 11.

The second is that the new AI features only extend back to the iPhone 15 Pro:

Apple Intelligence and Siri AI in iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27, watchOS 27, and visionOS 27 are available on iPhone 16 models or later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max.

The third says that some features are limited to just the latest and greatest models.

Apple’s most powerful on-device model and the features it enables, like expressive voices and more advanced dictation, are available on iPhone Air, iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The word ‘like’ is doing a lot of heavy lifting there: it means we don’t yet know what other features will fall into this category. Additionally, it’s not yet 100% clear whether phones that can’t perform these actions on-device will still get access to the same features, just relying on cloud connectivity.

This latter question is especially important when it comes to advanced dictation. However smart the new Siri may be, it first needs to understand what we are saying. The existing Siri speech-to-text capabilities fall way short of what is available from third-parties.

The overall model seems well-considered

Apple’s general approach here is to make Siri’s new capabilities transparently available system-wide. In other words, we can ask our iPhone to do something and the new Siri will step in to perform the task.

However, there are times when it’s useful to revisit an earlier chatbot session, and Apple allows us to do this through the Siri app. That seems to me the best of both worlds. We don’t need to open Siri to do anything requiring the new Apple Intelligence features, but we can access past sessions when required.

Agentic AI is key

The ability to ask our iPhone to carry out a task and have it be able to access not only the personal information we have stored on our phone, but also interact with apps, is absolutely key to truly useful AI.

Again, we will need to see how well this really works, but Apple does seem to be ticking all of the boxes in terms of the capabilities I was looking for.

Privacy is core

articles.title: New Game Trailer Contains A Jab At Gearbox’s Randy Pitchford As Payback Over A Borderlands 4 Joke
articles.subtitle: Borderlands Embracer Gearbox Randy Pitchford Saber Interactive Last month, Saber Interactive released the first trailer for its upcoming rideshare game, Rideshare Stimulator.
articles.author: Kotaku
articles.content:
Borderlands Embracer Gearbox Randy Pitchford Saber Interactive

Last month, Saber Interactive released the first trailer for its upcoming rideshare game, Rideshare Stimulator. The game appears to be a mix of Crazy Taxi and a more grounded taxi sim game, with some oddball writing and humor. It looks…fine. But the most interesting part of the trailer is a license plate that briefly appears and which, according to Saber’s CEO, is a direct shot at Gearbox CEO and co-founder Randy Pitchford and his infamous USB drive story.

As recently reported by Game File, the trailer for Rideshare Stimulator (yes, S timulator, not simulator) features a brief moment at around the 63-second mark that shows an SUV with a Texas license plate. The plate features the letters “USB,” a gear symbol, and then “DRV.”

This isn’t random. Borderlands developer Gearbox is located in Texas. And in 2018, Pitchford found himself in hot water after he left a USB drive behind at a Medieval Times restaurant. On the drive was a video he described as “barely legal porn” starring a woman who was “only 18.” This USB stick was part of a lawsuit against Gearbox filed by the studio’s former lawyer. The suit was settled in 2019.

But the story of Pitchford leaving behind a USB drive containing porn has never gone away and is referenced by people online to this day. And according to Saber CEO Matt Karch, Rideshare Stimulator is indeed directly referencing the USB boondoggle in its trailer, and it’s doing so as payback for what he believes was a dig at Saber and Gearbox’s former parent company, Embracer, found in Borderlands 4.

In that game, you can find a terrible location marked as “Embracer’s Bluff” that is filled with trash. Karch saw that location as a shot at Embracer, a company that many in the industry hate, but which the Saber CEO has defended.

“The dig is because Randy took shots at Embracer in Borderlands 4,” Karch told Game File when asked about the license plate. “Without Embracer, Randy is performing magic tricks at birthday parties for a living.”

Kotaku contacted Gearbox, but the studio declined to comment. Neither Take-Two nor Gearbox have ever confirmed with Kotaku that the Borderlands 4 location was a shot at Embracer.

As part of Embracer’s historic and infamous attempt to become a big publisher, the company bought up a bunch of studios, including Saber in 2020 and Gearbox in 2021. In late 2023, after everything started to collapse at Embracer when a massive deal fell through, both studios were sold. But at one point, the two companies were corporate siblings.

Pitchford has publicly been critical of Gearbox’s former parent company and even claimed that the story of Borderlands 4, which features an all-powerful maniac controlling everyone on a planet, was inspired by the studio’s time under Embracer.

“It’s amazing to me how fast people forget those who went above and beyond for them,” Karch told the outlet.

articles.title: Carbon Copy Cloner 7: The Mac Backup Software I Didn’t Know I Needed
articles.subtitle: Do you ever wonder if the grass is greener on the other side? If you’re happy with what you have, you probably don’t. But when something goes wrong — or you run into a particularly frustrating problem — it can be enough to make you start looking...
articles.author: OWC Rocket Yard
articles.content:
Do you ever wonder if the grass is greener on the other side? If you’re happy with what you have, you probably don’t. But when something goes wrong — or you run into a particularly frustrating problem — it can be enough to make you start looking elsewhere.

That’s exactly what happened when it came to the backup software on my Mac. I have used SuperDuper, from Shirt Pocket Software, for more than a decade now. It’s largely been reliable, to the point where I haven’t given it much thought.

That all changed a few days ago, when I ran into a particularly thorny issue with a routine SuperDuper backup procedure. The backup repeatedly failed, claiming that the destination drive had disconnected. This error happened multiple times, despite verifying that the cable and connections were both secure and in order.

I even reformatted the destination drive and started over from scratch. The result was the same. After troubleshooting in vain for several hours, I’d had enough. It was time to examine other backup options.

The chief competitor to SuperDuper is Carbon Copy Cloner (CCC) by Bombich Software. I’ve been aware of CCC for over 25 years. Truthfully, I had never given it much thought, as SuperDuper was meeting my needs. But after my backup issue, I decided it was time for me to give Carbon Copy Cloner a go, to really see if the grass was greener on the other side.

The first thing I noticed about Carbon Copy Cloner (version 7.x) is its polished interface. It feels like software that’s actively evolving alongside macOS. CCC feels like a modern Mac app. SuperDuper, while reliable, feels dated by comparison.

CCC keeps everything inside a single window. Tasks, connected volumes, scheduling, previews, restore options, and comparison tools are all easily accessible without feeling cluttered.

CCC’s onboarding is both thoughtful and well considered, especially for new users. CCC gently guides first-time users with contextual tooltips that explain what each option does. Once you’re comfortable, they can be disabled.

Setting up my first backup was very easy. Start off by creating a new Task. Next, select your source drive, followed by your destination drive. You can also create an automated backup schedule, with several granular options. I run backups daily, at a specific time, but if I wanted to, I could configure scheduled backups hourly, weekly, based on the day of the week, and more. All steps are explained in plain English.

(i. e. You don’t have to be Mac wizard to use it. ) Despite all the scheduling options, I never felt overwhelmed. The defaults are sensible, and advanced options stay out of your way until you need them.

I have my backup tasks configured as mirrors. If I delete a file on my source drive, CCC removes it from the backup during the next run.

CCC has several noteworthy features that are missing in SuperDuper.

Backup tasks can be paused at any time and resumed later. CCC includes Snapshots, which provide another layer of protection. Even if I accidentally delete a file that’s mirrored to my backup drive, I can often recover an earlier version from an APFS snapshot. CCC also includes a search feature to make it easy to find what you’re looking for across all of your snapshots. Unlike Carbon Copy Cloner, SuperDuper does not provide integrated APFS snapshot creation and management.

CCC can back up specific folders or entire disks, making it a one stop shop for duplication. CCC can target one source to multiple backup destinations. I really appreciate being able to view the copy and comparison results in real time, by way of a small integrated graph that appears during duplication.

Beyond cloning, Carbon Copy Cloner includes several robust pre-flight and post-flight automation options. It can also make local copies of cloud-only files, working with providers including Google Drive, iCloud, and OneDrive. I’ve found this especially useful now that services such as Backblaze don’t back up cloud-only placeholder files.

One of my favorite additions is the new Compare feature. It quickly highlights the differences between the source and destination before or after a backup, making it easy to verify exactly what’s going to change—especially when working with large drives.

Advanced Mac users will appreciate the conditional scheduling feature (i.e. run only on Ethernet, specific Wi-Fi networks,etc.)

So the real question is: should I buy Carbon Copy Cloner or SuperDuper?

articles.title: Preparing for next year’s Rosetta 2 demise
articles.subtitle: The reckoning is coming. Apple has done it before, and it’s doing it again. After macOS 27 Golden Gate, you will no longer be able to run legacy Intel apps using Rosetta 2.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
The reckoning is coming. Apple has done it before, and it’s doing it again. After macOS 27 Golden Gate, you will no longer be able to run legacy Intel apps using Rosetta 2. After the 26.4 update in March, when running any affected app in macOS 26 Tahoe, you see a notification banner when you launch affected software or a background component launches that uses Intel code:

Support Ending for Intel-based Apps. This version of “[App Name Here]” will not open in a future release of macOS. Learn how to update to an Apple silicon version. [Learn More pop-up menu]

There is one carveout noted for “certain older, unmaintained games that rely on Intel-based frameworks,” so far unnamed.

With information in hand, you can plan how to deal with Intel-only apps that have been abandoned, or the developers have seemingly no interest in updating. Printer makers are, so far, the worst.

A history of looking backward

Apple has done this before—many times, in fact. I’ve argued in the past that one of Apple’s key strengths, and a key to the continuity of the Mac’s operating system, is how well it’s managed transitions across chip architectures, frameworks, and operating system changes. 1

Look at what Apple has managed:

Motorola 680×0 to PowerPC (silent emulator)

Mac OS 9.1 (or later) to Mac OS X (Classic)

PowerPC to Intel (Rosetta, original flavor)

32-bit to 64-bit code (warnings)

Intel to Apple silicon M-series chips (Rosetta 2)

At each of those milestones, Apple offered either advance warnings about a future lack of compatibility, an emulator tool, or both. Does anyone have fond memories of running QuarkXPress using Classic in Mac OS X in its early days? When it crashed, which was often, it only took down the Classic “app” and didn’t require a Mac restart.

To be fair, Apple could have continued to let older software run for as long as it was willing to devote time to maintaining emulators or compatibility layers. We could be using apps written for Motorola 68030s on our M5 Macs right now! However, it makes increasingly less sense to support the past after a reasonable transition, particularly one that stretches years and sees the company discontinuing compatible hardware.

Apple released the last Intel-based model in August 2020, introduced its first M-series computer in November 2020, and halted sales of computers with Intel inside in 2023.

As part of this shift, you receive the Intel software warning, not just the first time you launch an affected app or an Intel-based component or even Terminal-accessed binary runs, but the next time you do it after a restart. Yes, it is trying to bug you to get a newer version of your software. Golden Gate also pulls an interesting trick: When you upgrade, it removes the Rosetta emulator. You’re prompted to install it the first time you need Intel code. I guess this is an extra spur to remind you.

Because Intel-only apps will continue to work under Rosetta until you install macOS 28 Dumbarton, these reminders will continue for at least another 16 months or so. 2 Once you upgrade to macOS 28, those apps and components will simply stop working.

Sunsets can be beautiful

Randy Smith Evergreen knows his immersive sims. As a designer on Thief: The Dark Project, he was there in the early days of the genre, and his credits include System Shock 2 and Dark Messiah: Might and Magic, as well as Thief 2 and Thief: Deadly Shadows. And he's pretty sure the genre is a bad fit for the AAA arms race.

"Myself and other folks who have worked extensively on immersive sims have a belief that the immersive sims that are being created today and are slated for the future are, by and large, thinking of themselves as [existing] in an arms race to be bigger and better," he tells us.

And this has been happening for a while. Just think about how Deus Ex: Mankind Divided pushed things in terms of fidelity. Or how big and expensive Arkane's modern offerings have been. They aren't competing with other immersive sims, they're competing with blockbuster shooters and vast open-world games from the biggest studios out there.

"Like, you just have to put more money into them, make a bigger and bigger immersive sim. It's got to be AAA, and it's got to sit right alongside Ghost of Tsushima and GTA 6, and it's got to be a game that's big enough to capture the public's attention. But I think that might be a misread for the audience size of immersive sims."

It certainly hasn't worked out for Arkane. Dishonored 2 and Prey are landmark immersive sims, but they were backed by a big publisher, Bethesda, who has since been swallowed up by Microsoft. Both games were considered commercial disappointments because Bethesda's expectations were not realistic for what has always been a niche genre.
